title: Module 9 Misconception Sort
intro: Decide whether each statement is true, false, or depends. These are the misconceptions that cost students points on exams.

items.s: A repeated-measures t test is just an independent t test with the same group measured twice.
items.why: The scores are dependent, so the correct analysis uses difference scores. Using the independent formula ignores the relationship between measures.

items.s: A repeated-measures design usually has more power than an independent-measures design with the same number of scores.
items.why: Removing stable individual differences shrinks the error term, particularly when the paired scores correlate.

items.s: For a related-samples test with 12 people measured twice, df = 22.
items.why: There are 12 difference scores, so df = 11.

items.s: Counterbalancing the order of conditions helps control order effects.
items.why: Half the participants do condition A first and half do B first.

items.s: A related-samples t test needs the difference scores to be roughly normal, or n large.
items.why: The distribution of mean differences should be approximately normal.

items.s: A significant related-samples t tells you every participant improved.
items.why: It tests the mean difference. Some individuals may not have changed or may have gotten worse.

items.s: A confidence interval gives the same information as a hypothesis test and nothing more.
items.why: It also shows the range of plausible effect sizes, which a p value alone does not.

items.s: Whether a pretest-posttest design with no control group shows that the treatment works
items.why: A significant improvement shows change over time. Without a comparison group, history, maturation, and testing effects could explain it.
